records.date: 2026-10-21 (Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence, Sec. AI in Finance, Vol. 9; DOI 10.3389/frai.2026.1969275; open access)

records.verification: FULL TEXT read (HTML) 2026-11-02 — abstract through conclusion with tables; references truncated. Title as published: 'The AI incident disclosure shadow: tracking AI incidents into U.S. securities filings'. DESIGN: pre-registered; 1,389 AI Incident Database incidents (2019-2026) linked to U.S.-listed issuers → 307 matched incidents across 21 issuers (Alphabet, Meta, Tesla, Microsoft dominate); filing universe = Forms 8-K/10-K/10-Q within 12 months of each incident (6/18/24-month windows tested in robustness); four-tier coding (T1 incident-specific, T2 legal-consequence only, T3 generic same-family language, T4 none); blind second coding; issuer-clustered bootstrap; retrieval audits. FINDINGS (exact): 'Only 4 incidents (1.3%; 95% CI 0.4-3.3) received incident-specific disclosure, and 7 (2.3%; 0.9-4.6) received any substantive disclosure'; 'The remaining 300 incidents (97.7%; 95.4-99.1) form an AI incident disclosure shadow'; 278 T3 incidents but only 84 matched both technology and harm families — '70.4% (64.9-75.4) of incidents had at most weakly related filing language'; substantive cases clustered on financial/legal channels (Zillow ~$304M write-down; GM Cruise '$478 million Cruise restructuring adjustment'); no detectable severity gradient (p = 0.61, power 23.3%); shadow rate 92.5-99.0% across robustness specs. LIMITS: AIID is media-derived — 'a conditional denominator... not population rates for all corporate AI incidents'; filing universe limited (non-repetition in filings != unavailability to investors); issuer attribution judgment; T2 lacks demonstrated inter-coder reliability (T1+T2 an upper bound); 'descriptive, not a legal-materiality or compliance determination'.

LIMITS: UK+EEA geographic scope only; shares published as bracketed ranges; not a global or Southeast Asia finding; the SMS designation is a recommendation, not yet a decision; the unverified 'voluntary commitments accepted' narrative circulating in secondary reporting is NOT on the official case page and is not used here. | TECHNICAL DEEPENING (Addendum 33, 2 Nov 2026): the final decision report's egress/switching analysis READ at paras 6.341-6.417 (PDF pp. 330-349); appendices L-Q (egress background, cost scenarios, free switching, customer views, internal documents, provider costs) located but NOT read. GEOGRAPHY AND DATE CHECKED: market scope 'UK+EEA' (fn 1); CMA's switching-cost scenario built on 'UK customer-level data on the mean volumes of data they stored for each year from 2018 to 2022' (para 6.406a, from AWS/Microsoft/Google information requests); list prices from provider websites 'for the applicable UK region' — 'London' region for Google and AWS — accessed 29 Jan 2024 (fn 1679-1680); provider egress-payment shares reported for 2023 (paras 6.349-6.352); free switching programmes introduced 2024 considered (para 6.344d). METHOD: one-off full-data-transfer scenario, cost expressed as % of annual spend spread over a typical three-year contract (para 6.406); provider-submitted alternatives (AWS customer-level analysis, Appendix M) given less weight because analyses based on customers who actually switched 'will tend to exclude any customers that found egress fees too high and were deterred from switching' (para 6.404) — a selection-bias critique. RESULTS (percentages REDACTED as [x-y] ranges in the public version): [0-5]% to [5-10]% of customers would pay egress fees above [5-10]% of annual spend per year over a three-year contract; the smallest customers (£1,000-£10,000/yr band) face the highest proportional fees; up-front (unspread): [10-20]% to [20-30]% of customers would face >[5-10]% of annual spend (paras 6.407-6.410). INTERPRETATION CAVEATS (paras 6.411-6.412): the analysis 'is likely to understate the effect of egress fees on switching' because total cloud spend includes non-data-intensive workloads; list prices ignore discounts (incl. CSA discounts, common among the largest customers) and premium alternatives (eg direct connect); 'the combined effect of these different factors is ambiguous'. records.title: Grids (Electricity 2026 chapter)
records.verification: full page read 2026-11-02.
records.relevance: The current IEA bottleneck account: over 2,500 GW of renewable, large-load and storage projects are stalled in grid queues worldwide. Annual grid investment needs to increase by approximately 50 percent by 2030 from today's USD 400 billion, alongside a scale-up in grid supply chains. Planning, permitting and completing new grid infrastructure takes 5 to 15 years, against 1 to 5 years for renewables projects, 1 to 3 years for data centres and 1 to 2 years for EV charging infrastructure, and prices for key grid components have nearly doubled over the past five years. Regulatory reforms and grid technologies together could free enough hosting capacity to connect between 1,200 and 1,600 GW of advanced-stage projects stuck in queues, with about 750 to 900 GW through conditional non-firm connection agreements and the remainder through grid-enhancing solutions. Grid-enhancing technologies alone (dynamic line rating, dynamic transformer rating, advanced power flow control, topology optimisation, storage as a transmission asset, plus reconductoring and voltage uprating) could unlock 450 to 700 GW, with the caveat that benefits cannot be stacked additively because several solutions address the same constraints. records.title: EU electricity grids

records.relevance: The EU briefing account: EU electricity infrastructure stretches over a million kilometres and is the most extensive and integrated grid in the world. Electricity is around 21 percent of final energy consumption, with demand projected to increase by 60 percent by 2030 and 64 GW of grid capacity to be added by 2030. Insufficient grid capacity led to congestion management costs of EUR 4.2 billion in 2023, while addressing missing cross-border links could decrease generation costs by EUR 9 billion annually to 2040 for EUR 6 billion annually of cross-border capacity and storage investment, and market integration already benefits consumers by up to EUR 34 billion every year. Grid-enhancing technologies are not included in planning by national regulatory authorities despite supplier claims of 20 to 40 percent overall network capacity increases by 2040 and 35 percent cost reductions compared with traditional expansion. The 6th PCI list of November 2023 includes 68 electricity projects (12 storage), 5 smart grid projects and 12 offshore projects. The TEN-E ten-year network development plan process takes up to two years, the 2022 plan is based on outdated assumptions according to ACER, and proposed projects in it amount to under EUR 10 billion per year, only 10 to 15 percent of actual annual investment needs. An average project takes more than 10 years to implement, about half of it permitting, with more than 500 GW of offshore capacity waiting for grid connection assessment. The Commission's EU Action Plan for Grids (November 2023) and a new European grids package expected in the coming months frame the policy section; later sections of the briefing are unknown from the sections read.

records.title: Energy and AI, Box 5.4: Water use by data centres
records.authors: Thomas Spencer and Siddharth Singh (lead authors)
records.verification: Box 5.4 page read 2026-11-02; rest of report left unread.
records.relevance: The global water baseline for AI infrastructure. Global data centre water consumption is around 560 billion litres per year (2023), rising to around 1,200 billion litres per year in 2030 in the Base Case. About two thirds of 2023 consumption comes from primary energy supply and electricity generation, one quarter from direct cooling, and the remainder from semiconductor and microchip manufacturing. An average 100 MW hyperscale data centre in the US consumes around 2 million litres per day in total, equivalent to about 6,500 households, with over 60 percent indirect. Solar PV and wind use one hundredth of the water of fossil sources or less. Almost 90 percent of manufacturing-stage water consumption is ultrapure water production, and chip manufacturing water consumption grows more than 50 percent from 2023 to around 70 billion litres in 2030. In Chinese Taipei, semiconductor manufacturers faced water restrictions during the 2021 drought. Around half of 2030 consumption is in Asia Pacific countries, where warm humid climates make cooling more water intensive. Microsoft's direct-cooling WUE for Asia Pacific was 1.65 L/kWh, more than three times its global average of around 0.5 L/kWh (Microsoft, 2022). The Climate Neutral Data Centre Pact targets WUE below 0.4 L/kWh by 2040, and the US average WUE was estimated at 0.36 L/kWh for 2023. Direct liquid cooling and immersion cooling can reduce direct water consumption significantly. AWS and Google have pledged to be water positive by 2030. Withdrawals are total water withdrawn, consumption is the portion not returned to the source. This record is a distinct Box 5.4 entry; the catalogue already has a separate iea-energy-and-ai record for the report as a whole, at a different URL.

records.title: 2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report
records.authors: Arman Shehabi, Sarah J. Smith, Alex Hubbard, Alex Newkirk, Nuoa Lei, Md Abu Bakar Siddik, Billie Holecek, Jonathan Koomey, Eric Masanet, and Dale Sartor
records.institution: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, US Department of Energy
records.verification: water section page read 2026-11-02 (report pp. 55-58, plus executive summary); rest of report left unread.
records.relevance: The measured US data centre water baseline. Direct water consumption rose from 21.2 billion litres in 2014 to 66 billion litres in 2023, with hyperscale and colocation accounting for 84 percent of the 2023 total and internal data centres falling to 12 percent (projected 2 percent by 2028). Hyperscale data centres in 2028 are expected to consume between 60 and 124 billion litres. The total indirect water footprint of US data centres was nearly 800 billion litres in 2023, attributed to electricity use. The 2023 national average indirect water intensity was 4.52 L/kWh (US overall electricity average 4.35 L/kWh) and emissions intensity 0.34 kg CO2e/kWh, with total GHG of 61 billion kg CO2e for that electricity. Method: bottom-up model from equipment shipments and installed base; indirect impacts estimated by linking data centre locations to balancing authorities using EIA hourly grid monitor (EIA 930), plant generation (EIA 923), water consumption and EPA emissions data (Siddik et al. 2024 method). The method does not incorporate power purchase agreements or behind-the-meter generation, and assumes the local balancing authority grid mix for all facilities in its jurisdiction.

records.title: Making AI Less 'Thirsty': Uncovering and Addressing the Secret Water Footprint of AI Models
records.authors: Pengfei Li, Jianyi Yang, Mohammad A. Islam, Shaolei Ren
records.institution: University of California, Riverside; University of Texas at Arlington
records.verification: abstract read 2026-11-02 (arXiv v1); paper body left unread.
records.relevance: The paper that made the AI water footprint concrete. Training GPT-3 in Microsoft's state-of-the-art US data centres can directly consume 700,000 litres of clean freshwater (enough for producing 370 BMW cars or 320 Tesla EVs), and consumption would have tripled if training were done in Microsoft's Asian data centres. The paper provides a principled methodology to estimate a fine-grained water footprint, discusses the spatial-temporal diversity of runtime water efficiency, and argues water and carbon footprints must be addressed together. The projection that global AI demand accounts for 4.2 to 6.6 billion cubic metres of water withdrawal in 2027 appears in the v5 abstract (2025-03-26 revision), not in the v1 abstract page read, so it is not recorded as a finding of this read. Accepted by Communications of the ACM; the v1 abstract is the record basis.

records.title: The carbon and water footprints of data centers and what this could mean for artificial intelligence

records.relevance: The disclosure audit that frames the water debate. The carbon footprint of AI systems alone could be between 32.6 and 79.7 million tons of CO2 emissions in 2025, while the water footprint could reach 312.5 to 764.6 billion litres. records.title: What are data centres and how sustainable are they?
records.institution: Parliamentary Office of Science and Technology (POST), UK Parliament
records.verification: summary and water and cooling sections page read 2026-11-02; rest of briefing left unread.
records.relevance: The UK parliamentary summary of data centre water use, useful for comparing UK figures with the IEA global figures. Data centres consume water three ways, from most to least direct: cooling systems, the electricity supply (gas and nuclear stations evaporate water), and semiconductor chip manufacturing (processed water to rinse wafers). The IEA estimate of global data centre water consumption around 560 billion litres per year rising to around 1,200 billion litres per year by 2030 is set against UK non-household water use of around 1,000 billion litres per year in 2024 to 2025. A techUK survey reported around half of data centres in England use water for cooling, the largest 4 percent of those use over 100 million litres per year, water efficiency was a low industry priority until recently, and drinking water is often the only commercial option available from UK water suppliers. Evaporated water is effectively non-renewable in the short term. Cooling table figures: chilled-water CRAH up to 25 million litres per MW per year, indirect free air cooling about 8 million litres per MW per year, evaporative or adiabatic about 1 to 8 million litres per MW per year depending on climate and method, direct free air near zero. Wording caution: the POSTnote summary phrases the 560 billion litre figure as in 2025, while the IEA report itself dates it to 2023; the IEA dating is used here.

records.title: Inside Microsoft's two-decade push to cut water intensity while scaling for growth
records.verification: full page read 2026-11-02.

In FY25 Microsoft replenished more water than it withdrew across global operations, ahead of its 2030 water positive commitment. Around 90 percent of the 2025 owned fleet operates with low- to zero-water cooling. The 2024 AI-optimised design consumes zero water for cooling via closed-loop direct-to-chip recirculation. Recycled, reused or non-potable shares: Quincy 74 percent, Singapore 99 percent, San Antonio 79 percent. Phoenix data centres improved WUE 23 percent year over year in FY25. records.title: Regulating Data Center Water Use in California
records.authors: Marie Grimm, Nell Green Nylen, and Michael Kiparsky
records.institution: Center for Law, Energy & the Environment (CLEE), UC Berkeley School of Law
records.verification: publication page read 2026-11-02 (overview and recommendations; full 63-page report left unread).
records.relevance: The US regulatory record for water: what reporting does and does not reveal. Existing reporting requirements have not provided a clear understanding of data centre water use in California, and lack of data hinders understanding of volumes, efficiency, sources, impacts and comparisons. Oversight of direct on-site water use relies on a patchwork of policies with gaps and inconsistencies. Levers for developers are siting in low water stress areas, cooling system choice, and recycled water, and more water-efficient cooling usually uses more energy. Local communities bear many impacts while local governments decide whether centres are built. Recommendations include expanded operator reporting of anticipated and actual water use regardless of source, state guidance and model regulations for local governments, requirements and incentives for efficiency and recycled water use, and site-specific water use data in corporate sustainability reports. Publication page is the record basis; the full 63-page report was not opened.

records.title: Water

records.title: Thirsty Data and the Lone Star State: The Impact of Data Center Growth on Texas' Water Supply
records.galaxy_topics: infrastructure/water, infrastructure/centres, infrastructure/electricity, politics/national, governance/rules, environment/resources
records.verification: executive summary read 2026-11-02; body chapters left unread.
records.relevance: The Texas case: where data centre water demand meets a state water plan that does not count it. As of September 2025 Texas has more than 400 data centre facilities (Baxtel count 464) concentrated in five regions (Dallas/Fort Worth 197, Houston 48, San Antonio 60, Austin 53, West Texas 59), requiring approximately 9,567 MW. Between direct on-site cooling and indirect electricity generation, existing Texas data centres consume approximately 25 billion gallons of water in 2025 (77 thousand acre-feet), 0.4 percent of total state water use. If growth projections hold, demand could rise to 29 to 161 billion gallons by 2030 (0.5 to 2.7 percent of annual state use). ERCOT estimates data centres could require 22,175 to 77,965 MW by 2030. The Texas State Water Plan does not include projected data centre demand growth, and Texas has no guidelines or requirements to address large water demands through efficiency, conservation or alternative supplies. Recommendations include requiring and releasing better electricity and water demand data, including large water demand uses in water planning, groundwater regulation reform, incentivising or requiring water reuse or conservation and offsets in the same river basin or aquifer, and public-private supply solutions.

records.title: Water Use and Community Trust: Key Components of Data Centers' Social License to Operate
records.verification: executive summary read 2026-11-02 plus introduction and key takeaways; body left unread.
records.relevance: The social licence record: why water becomes a siting constraint even when national volumes look small. While national-level water use from data centres remains relatively modest, localised impacts combined with limited transparency are driving rising community opposition and creating material risks to project development. Community acceptance is shaped less by absolute water volumes and more by perceptions of fairness, transparency, and long-term resource sustainability. Cooling technology choices involve unavoidable tradeoffs: water-efficient systems typically increase energy demand, while energy-efficient systems decrease direct water consumption but increase indirect water consumption. Indirect water use linked to thermoelectric power generation can exceed direct cooling water use by a factor of three (Siddik et al., 2021). An estimated 84 percent of data centre water consumption is attributable to hyperscale facilities, and Bloomberg News reports approximately two-thirds of data centers built or in development since 2022 are located in regions experiencing high levels of water stress (Bloomberg, 2025). Regulatory compliance alone is insufficient to secure community trust; projects that proactively engage stakeholders, adopt non-potable water strategies, and provide transparent, locally relevant information are more likely to achieve a durable social license to operate. The paper concludes that proactive water stewardship, including improved disclosure and early, meaningful community engagement, is essential not only for environmental performance but also for securing a durable social license to operate.

records.title: Large Energy Users Connection Policy
records.verification: executive summary read 2026-11-02; rest of the decision paper left unread.
records.relevance: Ireland's regulator decision that makes location an explicit connection condition for data centres, the siting complement to the earlier grid-connection records. The policy applies exclusively to data centres. A de minimis threshold of 1 MVA applies, below which only the location test applies. Connections from 1 to under 10 MVA must provide an autoproducer unit meeting 100 percent of maximum import capacity on a de-rated basis, participating in the wholesale market. Connections of 10 MVA and above must provide dispatchable onsite or proximate generation and/or storage matching maximum import capacity (de-rated), separately connected and metered, and cannot operate or ramp to full capacity before that generation is delivered. All connections at or above the de minimis must meet at least 80 percent of annual demand with additional renewable electricity generated in the Republic of Ireland, on a six-year glide path from energisation. On location, system operators must take into account whether the requested connection is in a constrained or unconstrained location, must publish up-to-date locational capacity information, and must publish a data centre connection process by 31 March 2026. The decision includes a new Section 34 direction superseding Direction CRU/21/124, the 2021 direction behind the de facto Dublin moratorium, and calls for a longer-term State-led approach encompassing spatial planning. Market intelligence cited suggests about 5.8 GW of additional data centre demand capacity in the medium term. The full decision paper's reasoning and conditions beyond the executive summary are unknown from this read.

records.relevance: The most detailed land evidence in this batch: a legislative audit of the world's largest data centre market. Northern Virginia holds 13 percent of reported global operational capacity and 25 percent of the Americas; the industry is estimated at 74,000 jobs, USD 5.5 billion labour income and USD 9.1 billion GDP annually, mostly from construction; a typical 250,000 sq ft centre has about 50 full-time workers; local revenue share in five mature localities ranged from under 1 percent to 31 percent. Access to power and large, flat areas of land are key site requirements. 29 percent of operational data centre properties are within 200 feet of residentially zoned property and 37 percent within 500 feet (131 sites across eight localities holding 93 percent of sites; Fairfax 55 percent within 200 feet and 70 percent within 500 feet; Loudoun 24 and 34 percent; Prince William 21 and 21 percent); over 60 percent are more than 500 feet away. Fairfax treated data centres as telecommunications facilities until 2021 and Loudoun originally as office use, so by-right development occurred next to homes. At least 15 sites (10 percent) generated noise complaints. A large campus site can take up to seven years to complete. JLARC recommends localities classify data centres as industrial uses, keep them from being too close to residential zones, and use setbacks and height limits. Method: proximity measured property line to nearest residential zoning using locality interactive maps; land conversion estimated from JLARC's inventory against USDA 2022 Census of Agriculture and National Land Cover Database data. records.verification: report page read 2026-11-02; disclaimer and team notes left unread.
records.relevance: An investor's framing of land itself as the scarce asset: 'powered land', sites where power capacity and land entitlement coincide. Every three to four MW of power capacity requires an acre of land (3.5 used as the average). About 20,000 acres of powered land sit under operational data centres worldwide now; another 40,000 acres (almost 2 billion sq ft) are needed over the next five years to support projected growth through 2030, just under three Manhattans or about 1.5 times Paris. records.title: Internet Exchange Points and Local Interconnection Ecosystems
records.verification: executive summary read plus key considerations sections 2026-11-03; remainder left unread.
records.relevance: The policy brief that frames the whole networks batch: why local interconnection, not just cables, decides whether access is affordable and resilient. Networks exchange traffic through transit (paid carriage), public peering at an Internet Exchange Point (IXP), and private peering; route servers let many networks peer multilaterally through one Border Gateway Protocol session, lowering barriers for smaller networks. IXPs keep local traffic local, cutting latency, transit cost and dependence on distant infrastructure, and they attract content caches, DNS infrastructure and time services that improve local availability. The brief's central warning is that interconnection is centralising: remote and virtual peering, hyperscale cloud infrastructure and distributed content delivery can complement local peering, but when they substitute for it, local IXPs lose participants and resilience falls. Regulatory risks named are telecommunications-style licensing of IXPs, critical-infrastructure or digital-sovereignty rules that undermine neutrality and voluntary peering, and sender-pays or fair-share traffic-payment proposals that change peering incentives. The brief argues policymakers should protect voluntary peering, neutral governance and diverse interconnection arrangements rather than simply promoting exchange infrastructure. A policy-advocacy document from the Internet Society, not a neutral empirical study; its affordability claims rest on cited Internet Society analysis.

records.title: Dissecting the Cost of Peering
records.verification: executive summary page read 2026-11-03; full study document left unread.
records.relevance: The evidence companion to the IXP policy brief: whether peering is actually cheaper than buying IP transit, and whether the savings reach users. The study combines public IXP port pricing with proprietary IP transit pricing from TeleGeography for 2018 to 2024 across multiple cities and countries, plus a survey of IXP operators finding port fees alone average 44 percent of total peering-related costs. Findings: peering is substantially cheaper than IP transit on average; larger peering cost savings are associated with lower broadband prices for consumers, expanded mobile network coverage and higher overall telecom revenues; benefits are most pronounced in moderately regulated economies and low- and lower-middle-income countries; and peering intensity, how much local networks actually participate in an IXP, drives outcomes more than the mere existence of an IXP. Recommendations: treat IXPs as strategic national infrastructure inside broadband and digital-economy strategies, prioritise support in low- and middle-income countries and moderately regulated markets, and improve visibility into the full cost structure of peering, not just port fees. Association findings, not causal proof, and the underlying transit prices are proprietary, so the cost comparison cannot be independently reproduced from this page.

records.title: Community-Driven IXPs
records.verification: full page read 2026-11-03; report document left unread.
records.relevance: The community-ownership angle on interconnection, focused on the Asia-Pacific region and developing regions. An IXP is a physical location where Internet service providers of various sizes, enterprise networks and content delivery networks exchange traffic locally, keeping local traffic local instead of routing it to far-off data centres. Community-driven IXPs are presented as fundamental to sustainable and resilient Internet infrastructure in developing regions, but facing limited access to finance and complex governance and operational problems. There is no one-size-fits-all model: commercial, nonprofit and community-driven IXPs serve different needs, and the report argues every economy benefits from having at least one community-driven IXP so infrastructure development aligns with community needs rather than commercial interests alone. The study draws on community-driven IXPs across the Asia-Pacific region to identify operational strategies and sustainable financial models. The landing page summarises the argument; the report's cases and financial detail were not read.

records.title: State of Mobile Internet Connectivity 2025
records.verification: press release page read 2026-11-03; full report left unread.
records.relevance: The global access baseline for the batch: coverage is nearly solved, use is not. In 2024, 4.7 billion people (58 percent of the world population) used mobile internet on their own device, up 200 million in the year, while 96 percent of the population lived within mobile internet coverage. Yet 3.1 billion people (38 percent) lived within coverage but did not use it, the Usage Gap, plus 300 million (4 percent) with no coverage at all, the Coverage Gap, leaving 3.4 billion unconnected. Over 90 percent of the unconnected live in low- and middle-income countries, where 93 percent of the unconnected are concentrated; rural adults in those countries are 25 percent less likely to use mobile internet than urban adults, and women 14 percent less likely than men. Barriers named are awareness, handset affordability (an entry-level internet-enabled device still costs 16 percent of average monthly income in low- and middle-income countries, 48 percent for the poorest 20 percent), digital skills, relevant content, security concerns and missing enablers such as electricity. GSMA argues a USD 30 handset could make devices affordable for up to 1.6 billion people, and estimates closing the usage gap would add USD 3.5 trillion in GDP by 2030. 5G covered 54 percent of the population and 4G 93 percent, with 4G rollout slowing as investment shifts to 5G. An industry-body account; the full report's methods and country tables were not read.

records.title: GSMA hails groundbreaking spectrum decisions at WRC-23
records.verification: full press release page read 2026-11-03.
records.relevance: The spectrum-allocation record for the batch, and the one place where an international treaty decision directly sets what networks can be built. At the ITU World Radiocommunication Conference 2023 in Dubai, governments agreed new mobile low-band spectrum (below 1 GHz) and mid-band spectrum in the 3.5 GHz and 6 GHz ranges. Final harmonisation of the 3.5 GHz band (3.3 to 3.8 GHz, the pioneer 5G band) was achieved across Europe, the Middle East and Africa and throughout the Americas. The 6 GHz band (6.425 to 7.125 GHz) was identified for mobile in every ITU region, with countries representing more than 60 percent of world population asking to be included; GSMA calls it the harmonised home for 5G-Advanced capacity expansion. WRC-23 also defined mobile use of more low-band spectrum in the 470 to 694 MHz band in Europe, the Middle East and Africa, which GSMA presents as a tool against the urban-rural divide because low-band signals cover wide, sparsely populated areas (in low- and middle-income countries, rural adults are 29 percent less likely to use mobile internet than urban adults). GSMA estimates 2 GHz of mid-band spectrum per market will be needed by 2030 to meet city demand. This is the mobile industry's welcoming reaction to the decisions, not the ITU conference record itself, and national implementation, which GSMA says is now the binding constraint, is unknown from this page.

records.title: Communications Ministry Tells Operators to Provide Signal Availability
records.authors: Secretariat of Cabinet of the Republic of Indonesia (Setkab)
records.institution: Secretariat of Cabinet of the Republic of Indonesia (Setkab)
records.verification: full page read 2026-11-03.
records.relevance: Indonesia's own government account of the moment its national backbone was finished, and a candid admission that backbone is not access. The Palapa Ring, also called Tol Langit (Sky Toll), a high-speed nationwide broadband network connecting Indonesia from Merauke in the east to Sabang in the west, was completed, and the Telecommunications and Information Accessibility Agency (BAKTI) managing director Anang Ahmad Latif used the occasion to press operators to solve signal availability. His argument: the Palapa Ring did not by itself resolve public signal availability, yet the sky toll was ready, so operators should use it, sell services at affordable prices and match Java speeds in frontier, outermost and least-developed (3T) and border regions. Building across the ocean costs three to four times a land project. Ten operators were already operating on the western and central Palapa Ring, while eastern operators were given three months of free trials. The government aimed at the 10 percent of the population in areas not feasible for business, with 4,000 base transceiver stations and multifunctional satellites planned so 4G signal would be available for real, against the problem that satellite transmission over 36,000 kilometres each way leaves latency the fibre ring cuts. A government statement at completion, not a later evaluation of whether operators delivered.

records.title: Singapore's Digital Connectivity Blueprint
records.verification: verified at origin 2026-11-03 (foreword, introduction, strategic priorities and international connectivity sections read; rest of report left unread).
records.relevance: Singapore's integrated masterplan for the whole digital infrastructure stack, the national-strategy counterpart to the Palapa Ring record. The Blueprint plans three layers together: hard infrastructure (submarine and satellite, broadband, mobile, Wi-Fi, data centres, cloud), physical-digital infrastructure (sensors, middleware, autonomous systems), and soft infrastructure (the Singapore Digital Utility Stack for identity, payments, invoicing, document verification and data exchange). Five strategic priorities: provide capacity for submarine cable landings to double within 10 years, potentially catalysing at least SGD 10 billion in submarine cable investment; build seamless end-to-end 10 Gbps domestic connectivity within five years through a tenfold Nationwide Broadband Network bandwidth increase, spectrum for faster Wi-Fi and for 5G Standalone networks; ensure world-class resilience and security of compute infrastructure; pioneer a roadmap for new green data centres (SGD 10 to 12 billion); and drive adoption of the Digital Utility Stack. On international connectivity, Singapore is already a leading submarine cable hub by number of cables landed and total capacity, and will intensify use of scarce landing space and resources so operators can diversify routes. Frontier moves include Low Earth Orbit satellite services for maritime and aviation, with sufficient spectrum for satellite systems and frameworks developed with the ITU on LEO and non-LEO coexistence. Background in the report: nationwide fibre-to-the-home since 2013, 95 percent outdoor coverage on the first two 5G Standalone networks by end 2022, and 99 percent of households with internet access as of 2022. A government plan document; delivery against the 10-year targets is unknown from this report.

records.title: International Advisory Body on Submarine Cable Resilience: Report of the Working Groups
records.authors: International Telecommunication Union (ITU) and International Cable Protection Committee (ICPC)
records.institution: International Telecommunication Union (ITU) and International Cable Protection Committee (ICPC)
records.verification: executive summary read 2026-11-03; working group chapters left unread.
records.relevance: The resilience-governance record for the batch: what the world agreed, after the cable incidents of 2024 to 2025, about protecting the infrastructure that carries over 99 percent of intercontinental data traffic. The International Advisory Body on Submarine Cable Resilience was established in 2024 by the ITU with the ICPC, co-chaired by Nigeria and Portugal, with three working groups: timely deployment and repair; risk identification, monitoring and mitigation; and fostering connectivity and geographical diversity. Executive summary findings: cables remain highly exposed to fishing, anchoring, natural hazards and seabed congestion, and while many disruptions are accidental their impact is significant where redundancy is limited; restoration and repair timelines are increasing in some regions because of complex permitting, fragmented regulation, limited repair vessels and operational constraints; geographical concentration through a limited number of maritime chokepoints and cable corridors creates systemic vulnerability; small island developing states, least developed countries and other underserved regions depend on a small number of systems; and changing weather patterns affect coastal landing infrastructure, seabed stability and long-term planning. Recommendations: stronger risk identification, monitoring and incident response; greater route diversity and redundancy; government-industry-international cooperation; investment and financing mechanisms; capacity building, especially in developing countries and vulnerable regions; and protection of cables within broader critical-infrastructure frameworks. The Abuja (February 2025) and Porto (February 2026) summit declarations accompany the report. The working group chapters' evidence and country detail were not read.

records.title: Gigabit Infrastructure Act
records.verification: full page read 2026-11-03.
records.relevance: Europe's deployment-rules record: the law that tries to make building fast networks cheaper by fixing permits and sharing, rather than by funding alone. The Gigabit Infrastructure Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1309) replaces the 2014 Broadband Cost Reduction Directive, which a 2018 report and evaluation found was not applied consistently across the EU. It aims for faster, cheaper and simpler rollout of very high-capacity networks through shared use of existing ducts and poles, co-deployment and coordination of civil works so telecom operators can lay fibre alongside public works, streamlined administrative procedures for network rollout, and high-speed-ready infrastructure in buildings with access to it. It also seeks a smaller environmental footprint by favouring fibre and 5G and reusing existing physical infrastructure. The act serves the 2030 Digital Decade connectivity target of cross-EU gigabit access and fast mobile data in all populated areas. Per the current page, the act fully applies as of 12 May 2026, monitoring indicators were finalised by November 2025, and a Commission report is planned for May 2028. In parallel, the February 2024 Gigabit Recommendation guides national regulators on access remedies for operators with significant market power and on the copper-to-fibre transition. Whether streamlined permits actually accelerated rollout is unknown from this policy page.

records.title: Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment (BEAD) Program: BEAD Supplemental Deployment Policy Notice
records.institution: National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA), United States
records.verification: full page read 2026-11-03.
records.relevance: The United States' universal-broadband record at its current stage: the largest public broadband programme in American history, now dealing with the locations its first round missed. The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act of 2021 established the Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment (BEAD) programme with USD 42.45 billion to ensure broadband availability throughout the United States, administered by NTIA. By this September 2026 notice, all final proposals required by the Act had been approved, and NTIA allowed states, territories and the District of Columbia to access additional BEAD funding for locations that may remain unserved because of defaults in other federal or state programmes, misreporting by providers, and changes to the Federal Communications Commission's broadband maps since final proposals were completed. The notice modifies and replaces certain requirements of the May 2022 BEAD Notice of Funding Opportunity, while the rest of that notice and the BEAD Restructuring Policy Notice remain in place. The notice page itself is short; the underlying funding allocations, technology mix and build timelines are not in this read.

records.title: Emboldened offenders, endangered communities: internet shutdowns in 2024
records.verification: press release page read 2026-11-03; full report left unread.
records.relevance: The deliberate-disruption record for the batch: networks as something governments switch off, not only something that breaks. In 2024, authorities imposed at least 296 internet shutdowns in 54 countries, the worst year on record and a 35 percent increase over the previous high in 2022. Myanmar imposed the most (85 shutdowns, by at least six perpetrators led by the military regime), followed by India (84); India, Myanmar, Pakistan and Russia together account for at least 203 shutdowns, 69 percent of the global total. Conflict was the leading trigger for a second year (at least 103 conflict-related shutdowns in 11 countries), followed by protests (74), exams (16) and elections (12). A record 71 platform blocks were recorded in 35 countries, with X the most blocked platform. Seven countries shut down the internet for the first time: Comoros, El Salvador, France, Guinea-Bissau, Malaysia, Mauritius and Thailand. Cross-border shutdowns rose to 25 imposed by eight offenders affecting people in 13 countries. Counterpoints noted: the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights adopted a resolution urging members not to shut down the internet during elections, Mauritius rescinded a social media ban during its election, and world leaders at the 2024 UN Summit of the Future committed to refrain from shutdowns. The press release summarises the report; its country narratives and verification methods were not read.

records.title: Meaningful connectivity: What creates a successful community network?
records.date: 2025 (no explicit date on page read; first part in the October Intermedia issue, after the September 2024 Summit of the Future)
records.verification: full page read 2026-11-03.
records.relevance: The bottom-up access record: what community-built networks actually need to survive, from a consultation with about 350 community networks in 2023 and 2024 across the global south. Twelve principles recur across successful projects, including community-needs focus, participatory design and operation, community ownership through participation, governance and management, gender equality at the core, and environmental and cultural awareness. An APC survey of community-centred connectivity networks found 149 independent initiatives with 342 sites in 32 countries: 59 percent provide in-premises connectivity via Wi-Fi hotspots, 21 percent broadband via public Wi-Fi, and only 5 percent through 2G, 3G or 4G networks; 71 percent run capacity-building training, 59 percent personal support, 17 percent connect schools. Cases in the article's table include TunapandaNET in Kenya, Zenzeleni in South Africa, Telecomunicaciones Indigenas Comunitarias in Oaxaca, Mexico, the Nasa community Wind Network in Colombia, Ciptagelar in West Java, Indonesia, and B4RN, a cooperative fibre network in rural England. The binding constraints are policy, not technology: spectrum access (no use-it-or-share-it provision for licensed spectrum unused in rural areas, unaffordable LTE bands, auctions built for incumbents; Mexico's 2013 reform and a Supreme Court ruling waiving spectrum fees for indigenous community networks are the cited exceptions), onerous licensing, backhaul as the largest single operating cost, scarce universal-service and financing mechanisms, missing open local data, energy, skills, and gendered barriers to participation. The article argues technology, community creativity and claims for equality are moving faster than the policy arenas holding community networks back, and ties the agenda to the UN Summit of the Future's commitment to close all digital divides.

records.title: Palapa Ring has successfully improved mobile connectivity in remote Indonesian islands
records.verification: full page read 2026-11-03.
records.relevance: The independent-measurement companion to the government Palapa Ring record: whether the backbone actually changed users' experience. Opensignal compared its users' mobile network experience across 12 Indonesian regions, covering all seven archipelagos, between the third quarter of 2018 and the third quarter of 2020. 4G Availability rose everywhere: Sulawesi gained 15.4 percentage points, Sumatra, Maluku and Papua 14 to 15 points, while Jakarta Raya, starting highest, rose 8 points to 94.1 percent; most regions reached 90 to 91 percent or above, with Papua at 88.8 percent and Kalimantan at 87.1 percent. Download Speed Experience rose most in Papua (87 percent), Jakarta Raya (78 percent) and Kalimantan (78 percent), and least in Maluku (26 percent); Jakarta Raya led at 13.6 Mbps, just ahead of Papua (13.1 Mbps), Nusa Tenggara (12.8 Mbps) and Maluku (12.6 Mbps). Video Experience improved most in Papua (36 percent) and moved every region except Jawa Tengah from Fair to Good on Opensignal's 100-point scale. The article itself cautions that the improvement reflects, among other factors, operators taking advantage of the Palapa Ring, so the gains are not attributed to the backbone alone, and whether remote-island experience keeps pace with the capital region depends on continued base-station deployment as demand grows. A measurement firm's user-experience data, not a representative national survey.

records.title: Article 72: Post-market monitoring by providers and post-market monitoring plan for high-risk AI systems
records.verification: verified-at-origin 2026-11-03 (Article 72 text as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 read via unofficial consolidated version; EUR-Lex original returned an empty body; Article 73 deadlines left unread).
records.relevance: The post-market half of AI accountability under the EU AI Act. Article 72 requires providers of high-risk AI systems to establish and document a post-market monitoring system proportionate to the nature of the AI technology and its risks, actively and systematically collecting, documenting and analysing relevant data from deployers and other sources throughout the system's lifetime, so the provider can evaluate continuing compliance with the Act's Chapter III, Section 2 requirements, including analysis of interaction with other AI systems. The system must rest on a post-market monitoring plan that forms part of the Annex IV technical documentation; the Commission is to adopt guidance, including a template, by 2 September 2027. Where a sectoral Union harmonisation regime already requires such a system and plan, providers may integrate the Article 72 elements into the existing ones. The text read is the unofficial consolidated version as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (the Digital Omnibus on AI), current to 29 October 2026; the EUR-Lex original returned an empty body when fetched, so this record relies on that consolidation and is labelled as such. Chapter IX also contains Article 73 on reporting serious incidents, but the Article 73 page was blocked by a bot check, so its reporting deadlines are deliberately not recorded here.

records.title: Defective products: liability (Directive (EU) 2024/2853)
records.verification: verified-at-origin 2026-11-03 (full EUR-Lex summary page read).
records.relevance: The EU's no-fault liability route for AI harm. Directive (EU) 2024/2853 rewrites EU product liability for the software era: software, including AI systems, is expressly a product, whatever the supply mode, and the manufacturer remains liable for defects emerging from updates or upgrades performed under its control, and from an AI system's continuous learning while it remains under the manufacturer's control. Digital services necessary for the product to function, incorporated under the manufacturer's control, are covered too. Liability is no-fault: the victim proves defect, damage and the causal link. Compensable damage covers death and personal injury, including medically recognised damage to psychological health, damage to property, and destruction or corruption of data not used for professional purposes. Where the manufacturer is outside the EU, importers, authorised representatives and, failing those, fulfilment service providers can be held liable, and platforms acting as economic operators face the same liability. Both parties can seek access to evidence. Liability runs 10 years from placing on the market, 25 years for latent personal injuries, with three years to bring a claim. Member states must transpose by 9 December 2026, and the rules apply to products placed on the market or put into service from that date; earlier products stay under the 1985 directive.

records.title: Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (CETS No. 225)
records.verification: verified-at-origin 2026-11-03 (preamble, Articles 1 to 14 and Articles 29 to 36 read; Articles 15 to 28 left unread).
records.relevance: The first legally binding international AI treaty. The Council of Europe Framework Convention (CETS No. 225), opened for signature at Vilnius on 5 September 2024, requires parties to keep AI lifecycle activities consistent with human rights, democracy and the rule of law, with measures graduated to the severity and probability of adverse impacts. Its scope covers public authorities and private actors acting on their behalf, and requires parties to address risks from other private actors in line with the Convention's object and purpose. Article 9 is the accountability clause: parties must adopt or maintain measures to ensure accountability and responsibility for adverse impacts on human rights, democracy and the rule of law. Article 14 requires accessible and effective remedies for human rights violations from AI lifecycle activities, including documentation of relevant information about systems that may significantly affect human rights, information sufficient for affected persons to contest decisions made or substantially informed by the system, and an effective possibility to complain to competent authorities. Article 30 sets entry into force at five consenting signatories including at least three Council of Europe member states, three months later. The preamble, Articles 1 to 14 and Articles 29 to 36 were read; the middle articles, including the follow-up mechanism, were not.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence Accountability Policy Report
records.authors: Ellen P. Goodman (principal author), National Telecommunications and Information Administration
records.institution: National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA), US Department of Commerce
records.verification: verified-at-origin 2026-11-03 (executive summary, report pages 1 to 5, read; body chapters left unread).
records.relevance: The US government's fullest statement of what AI accountability would require in practice. NTIA's March 2024 report, written after an April 2023 request for comment that drew over 1,400 comments, conceives accountability as a chain: information flow (documentation, disclosures and access) supports independent evaluation (including red-teaming and audits), which feeds into consequences (liability, regulation, market pressure). Its eight recommendations, grouped as Guidance, Support and Regulatory Requirements, call for federal guidelines for AI audits and auditors, standardised model and system disclosures in plain language, recommendations on applying and supplementing liability rules across the AI value chain, registries of high-risk deployments, adverse incidents and audits, stronger cross-sectoral government capacity, and requirements that federal contractors and grantees adopt sound AI governance and assurance practices. The executive summary was read in full; the body chapters were not, so the report's detailed evidence and sector discussion are not summarised here.

records.title: The OECD AI Incidents Monitor: an evidence base for effective AI policy
records.verification: verified-at-origin 2026-11-03 (full explainer page read; live monitor interface left unread).
records.relevance: The evidence base behind incident accountability. The OECD AI Incidents Monitor (AIM) scans media from 150,000 news sources in real time, collecting over one million stories a day through the EventRegistry platform, and auto-classifies AI incidents and hazards by sector, country, stakeholders affected, severity and harm type, using filters consistent with the OECD Framework for Classifying AI Systems. The explainer argues incident reports are rising rapidly, media reports are only the tip of the iceberg, and without a shared definition and compatible reporting, policymakers lack the evidence base for regulation; AIM is meant to feed a future global monitor for standardised incident reporting and a common reporting framework developed with the OECD Expert Group on AI Incidents. A search example shows generative AI incidents growing rapidly since November 2022. This record covers the OECD's launch explainer page, not the live monitor interface, and no current incident total is stated because the page gives none.

records.title: The AI Incident Database
records.verification: verified-at-origin 2026-11-03 (full about page read; incident listings themselves left unread).
records.relevance: The public ledger of AI failures that other accountability mechanisms cite. The AI Incident Database, launched by the Partnership on AI in 2020 and now run by the Responsible AI Collaborative, indexes the collective history of harms or near harms realised in the real world by deployed AI systems, explicitly modelled on aviation accident databases and the CVE system for software vulnerabilities. Its initial set of over 1,000 incident reports was deliberately broad: an autonomous car killing a pedestrian, a trading algorithm causing a flash crash, a facial recognition system causing a wrongful arrest. Anyone may submit reports, which editors review and index; researchers are invited to use the Discover application to find how deployed systems produced unexpected outcomes before deploying similar ones. The about page was read in full; the incident listings themselves were not opened, so no current count or case is claimed here.

records.title: Directive on Automated Decision-Making
records.verification: verified-at-origin 2026-11-03 (full 2021 edition PDF read; Treasury Board page itself rejected the request; later amendments left unverified).
records.relevance: The earliest national AI accountability regime in the batch, and the most operationally detailed. Canada's Directive on Automated Decision-Making, in effect 1 April 2019 with compliance required by 1 April 2020, binds federal institutions using automated decision systems in production to make or support administrative decisions about clients, excluding test environments and national security systems. Its central mechanism is the Algorithmic Impact Assessment, completed before production and published by default, which scores a system into impact levels I to IV. Obligations scale with level: notice in plain language, a meaningful explanation (for levels II and above, for common results; for III and IV, with any denial of a benefit, service or regulatory action), peer review (none at level I, at least one qualified expert at level II, at least two at levels III and IV, or a data and automation advisory board), human intervention points with the final decision made by a human at levels III and IV, and approval by the Deputy Head (III) or the Treasury Board (IV). Departments must also test for unintended bias before launch, monitor outcomes, document decisions, provide recourse options, and report on effectiveness; non-compliance consequences fall under the Financial Administration Act. The 2021 edition of the directive was read in full; the Treasury Board's own directive page rejected the fetch, and any later amendments were not verified at origin.

records.title: Automated Employment Decision Tools (AEDT)
records.authors: New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection
records.institution: New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP)
records.verification: verified-at-origin 2026-11-03 (full DCWP page read).
records.relevance: The first US law to regulate AI hiring tools directly. New York City Local Law 144 of 2021 prohibits employers and employment agencies from using an automated employment decision tool unless the tool has had an independent bias audit within the past year, information about the audit is publicly available, and required notices have been given to employees or job candidates. The Department of Consumer and Worker Protection began enforcement on 5 July 2023, and its roundtable materials clarify that notice must be given 10 business days before use. The agency page also gives a complaint route for tools used without the audit, the published summary, or the notices. The page states the three conditions; it does not describe any duty to change a tool in response to audit results, and no penalties or enforcement outcomes are claimed here because the page does not state them.

records.title: SB26-189: Automated Decision-Making Technology
records.verification: verified-at-origin 2026-11-03 (full legislature bill summary read; signing date left unstated on the page).
records.relevance: The current Colorado AI law, replacing the 2024 act with a narrower set of duties. SB26-189 repeals and reenacts the consumer protections enacted by SB24-205 in 2024. The new act defines automated decision-making technology broadly, covering systems that process personal data and use computation to generate outputs used to make, guide or assist decisions, and applies to consequential decisions about education, employment, housing, financial or lending services, insurance, health care, and essential government services and public benefits. From 1 January 2027, developers of covered systems must give deployers technical documentation on intended uses, training-data categories, known limitations and instructions for appropriate use and human review, and notify deployers of material updates; deployers must give clear notice at the point of interaction, a plain-language description of the system's role within 30 days after an adverse consequential decision, and offer consumers the right to request and correct personal data and to seek meaningful human review and reconsideration. The Attorney General must adopt rules clarifying the post-adverse-outcome disclosures by 1 January 2027, enforces through the Colorado Consumer Protection Act with a violation deemed a deceptive trade practice, must give 60 days' notice and opportunity to cure before actions brought before 1 January 2030, and the act creates no new private right of action. The legislature's summary page does not give a signing date, so none is stated.

records.title: Keep your AI claims in check
records.authors: Michael Atleson, FTC Division of Advertising Practices
records.verification: verified-at-origin 2026-11-03 (full blog post read).
records.relevance: The US consumer-protection baseline for AI marketing. In this February 2023 business guidance, the FTC's Division of Advertising Practices warns marketers not to overpromise what an algorithm or AI tool can deliver, since false or unsubstantiated efficacy claims are, in its words, its bread and butter. Four questions frame enforcement: are you exaggerating what the product can do, beyond what any current AI can do; are you claiming superiority over a non-AI product without adequate proof; do you know the reasonably foreseeable risks and impact before putting the product on the market, without blaming a third-party developer or pleading that the technology is a black box; and does the product actually use AI at all, since merely using an AI tool in development is not the same as a product having AI in it, and FTC technologists can look under the hood. The full post was read; it is guidance under the FTC Act's ban on deceptive practices, not a rule.

records.title: SEC Charges Two Investment Advisers with Making False and Misleading Statements About Their Use of Artificial Intelligence
records.verification: verified-at-origin 2026-11-03 (full press release read).
records.relevance: The first SEC AI-washing enforcement, and the market-disclosure counterpart to the FTC's advertising guidance. On 18 March 2024 the SEC settled charges against Delphia (USA) Inc. and Global Predictions Inc. for false and misleading statements about their use of AI. Delphia claimed from 2019 to 2023 in filings, a press release and on its website to use machine learning and client data to predict winning companies and trends, when it did not have the capabilities claimed; Global Predictions falsely claimed in 2023 to be the first regulated AI financial advisor and to offer expert AI-driven forecasts. Both were charged under the Advisers Act and the Marketing Rule, censured and ordered to cease and desist, settling without admitting or denying the findings: Delphia paid a $225,000 civil penalty and Global Predictions $175,000, $400,000 in total. The full press release was read.

records.title: Joint Statement on Enforcement Efforts Against Discrimination and Bias in Automated Systems
records.authors: Rohit Chopra (CFPB), Kristen Clarke (US DOJ Civil Rights Division), Charlotte A. Burrows (EEOC), Lina M. Khan (FTC)
records.institution: CFPB, US DOJ, EEOC and FTC (joint)
records.verification: verified-at-origin 2026-11-03 (full joint statement PDF read).
records.relevance: Four US enforcement agencies speaking together on AI discrimination. In April 2023 the heads of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and the Federal Trade Commission issued a joint statement that existing civil rights, consumer protection and competition law already applies to automated systems, defined broadly as software and algorithmic processes, including AI, used to automate workflows and decisions. It names three sources of unlawful discrimination: unrepresentative or historically biased datasets and correlations with protected classes; model opacity, where even the developer cannot explain a black-box system, making fairness hard to assess; and design and use, where developers misunderstand the context in which a tool will be deployed. The statement records each agency's existing tools, including the CFPB's position that a technology being too complex, opaque or new is no defence to a credit-law violation, the DOJ's Fair Housing Act position on algorithm-based tenant screening, the EEOC's disability-rights guidance on employment AI, and the FTC's algorithmic disgorgement remedy, requiring destruction of models trained on improperly collected data. It states expressly that it creates no new rights or obligations and is not enforceable. The full statement was read.
