records.title: Mata v. Avianca, Inc.: Opinion and Order on Sanctions
records.authors: P. Kevin Castel, US District Judge
records.institution: US District Court for the Southern District of New York
records.verification: verified-at-origin 2026-11-03 (introduction, findings of fact and penalty conclusions read; remainder left unread).
records.relevance: The case that made AI verification a professional duty. In Mata v. Avianca, Judge P. Kevin Castel of the Southern District of New York sanctioned two lawyers and their firm under Rule 11 after they filed a brief citing judicial opinions invented by ChatGPT, complete with fabricated quotations and internal citations, and stood by the fake opinions after the court questioned their existence and ordered production of the cases. The opinion holds there is nothing inherently improper about using a reliable AI tool for assistance, but existing rules impose a gatekeeping role on attorneys to ensure the accuracy of their filings; the court found bad faith based on conscious avoidance and false and misleading statements, and imposed a $5,000 penalty, jointly and severally, paid into the Registry of the Court, as sufficient but not more than necessary for specific and general deterrence. The opinion was read via the CourtListener/RECAP republication; the introduction, findings of fact and penalty conclusions were read, and the remainder was not.

records.title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
records.authors: Woosuk Kwon, Zhuohan Li, Siyuan Zhuang, Ying Sheng, Lianmin Zheng, Cody Hao Yu, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Hao Zhang, Ion Stoica
records.verification: abstract read 2026-11-03; paper body left unread.
records.relevance: The serving paper behind vLLM, the system that made paged KV cache management standard. High-throughput LLM serving needs large batches, but each request's key-value (KV) cache is huge and grows and shrinks dynamically, so naive management wastes memory through fragmentation and redundant duplication and caps batch size. PagedAttention borrows virtual memory paging from operating systems: the KV cache is split into fixed-size blocks that can sit in non-contiguous physical memory, with near-zero waste and sharing of blocks within and across requests. The vLLM system built on it improves throughput of popular LLMs by 2 to 4 times at the same latency compared with FasterTransformer and Orca, with larger gains for longer sequences, larger models and more complex decoding. The abstract is the record basis; the paper body was not read.

records.title: FlashAttention-2: Faster Attention with Better Parallelism and Work Partitioning
records.verification: abstract read 2026-11-03; paper body left unread.
records.relevance: The kernel optimisation that made long-context attention cheap enough to serve. The attention layer is the bottleneck in scaling Transformers to longer sequences because its runtime and memory grow quadratically with sequence length. FlashAttention exploits the asymmetric GPU memory hierarchy to cut memory to linear in sequence length and speed up runtime 2 to 4 times over optimised baselines, with no approximation, by tiling and never materialising the full attention matrix in high-bandwidth memory. FlashAttention-2 fixes the first version's weak spot, suboptimal work partitioning across thread blocks and warps, which left it at only 25 to 40 percent of theoretical peak FLOPs per second. It reduces non-matmul FLOPs, parallelises attention even for a single head across thread blocks, and distributes work across warps to cut shared-memory traffic, reaching around 2 times the speed of FlashAttention, 50 to 73 percent of peak FLOPs per second on A100, and 225 TFLOPs per second when training GPT-style models end to end. The abstract is the record basis; the paper body was not read.

records.title: Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding
records.authors: Yaniv Leviathan, Matan Kalman, Yossi Matias
records.verification: abstract read 2026-11-03; paper body left unread.
records.relevance: The draft-then-verify trick that speeds up autoregressive decoding without changing outputs. Decoding K tokens normally takes K serial runs of the model. Speculative decoding uses a small, efficient approximation model to draft several candidate tokens, then runs the large target model once in parallel over those candidates, accepting them under a sampling rule that preserves the target model's output distribution exactly. It needs no retraining or architecture change and works on off-the-shelf models. Demonstrated on T5-XXL, it gives 2 to 3 times acceleration over the standard T5X implementation with identical outputs. The abstract is the record basis; the paper body was not read. DeepMind's independent speculative sampling paper (Chen et al., arXiv:2302.01318) reported 2 to 2.5 times on Chinchilla 70B but was not separately opened.

records.title: GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers
records.authors: Elias Frantar, Saleh Ashkboos, Torsten Hoefler, Dan Alistarh
records.verification: abstract read 2026-11-03 (arXiv v1); paper body left unread; v2 figures not recorded.
records.relevance: The one-shot quantisation method that made 4-bit LLM inference practical. Large GPT-style models are expensive to store and run: even inference can need several high-end GPUs. GPTQ is a one-shot weight quantisation method based on approximate second-order (Hessian) information that quantises a 175-billion-parameter model in about four GPU hours down to 3 or 4 bits per weight with negligible accuracy loss versus the uncompressed baseline, more than doubling the compression of earlier one-shot methods and allowing a 175-billion-parameter model to run on a single GPU for generative inference. The v1 abstract reports end-to-end inference speedups over FP16 of around 2 times on A100 and 4 times on A6000; the later v2 abstract reports higher figures, which are deliberately not recorded here because only v1 was read. GPTQ's gains come from reduced memory movement, not fewer computations, and the study covers generative tasks only, not activation quantisation. The v1 abstract is the record basis; the paper body was not read.

records.title: AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration
records.authors: Ji Lin, Jiaming Tang, Haotian Tang, Shang Yang, Wei-Ming Chen, Wei-Chen Wang, Guangxuan Xiao, Xingyu Dang, Chuang Gan, Song Han
records.institution: MIT; Tsinghua University; Shanghai Jiao Tong University
records.verification: abstract read 2026-11-03 (arXiv v5, MLSys 2024 version); paper body left unread.
records.relevance: The activation-aware counterpart to GPTQ, and the route to LLMs on phones. Not all weights matter equally: protecting only about 1 percent of salient weight channels greatly reduces quantisation error, but salience must be judged from the activation distribution, not the weights. AWQ scales up the salient channels through an equivalent transformation, avoiding hardware-inefficient mixed precision, and needs no backpropagation or reconstruction, so it generalises across domains and modalities without overfitting its calibration set. It beats prior work on language modelling and domain benchmarks (coding, math), works for instruction-tuned and, for the first time, multi-modal models, and its companion TinyChat framework offers more than 3 times speedup over Hugging Face FP16 on desktop and mobile GPUs, including running a 70-billion-parameter Llama-2 model on a mobile GPU. The v5 abstract (MLSys 2024 best paper version) is the record basis; the paper body was not read.

records.title: Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models
records.authors: Gyeong-In Yu, Joo Seong Jeong, Geon-Woo Kim, Soojeong Kim, Byung-Gon Chun
records.verification: USENIX page abstract read 2026-11-03; paper body left unread.
records.relevance: The origin of continuous batching, the scheduling idea underneath modern LLM serving. Autoregressive generation runs the model once per output token, but existing serving systems batched whole requests: a finished request could not return until its whole batch finished, and a new request had to wait for the current batch to complete. Orca introduces iteration-level scheduling, invoking the execution engine for a single model iteration on the current batch and re-deciding the batch each iteration, plus selective batching, which applies batching only to a selected set of operations so it composes with Transformer attention. The resulting distributed system, designed for models with hundreds of billions of parameters, shows 36.9 times throughput improvement at the same latency as NVIDIA FasterTransformer on GPT-3 175B. Note: an arXiv identifier circulating for this paper (2203.08913) resolves to a different paper, Memorizing Transformers, so this record uses the USENIX proceedings page, which is the paper's actual home. The USENIX abstract is the record basis; the paper body was not read.

records.title: SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs
records.authors: Lianmin Zheng, Liangsheng Yin, Zhiqiang Xie, Chuyue Sun, Jeff Huang, Cody Hao Yu, Shiyi Cao, Christos Kozyrakis, Ion Stoica, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Clark Barrett, Ying Sheng
records.institution: University of California, Berkeley; Stanford University (LMSYS)
records.verification: abstract read 2026-11-03; paper body left unread.
records.relevance: The serving system for multi-call LLM programs: agents, reasoning chains, retrieval pipelines and structured output. Such programs need many generation calls, control flow and structured inputs and outputs, but existing engines discard each request's KV cache when it finishes, so repeated prefixes are recomputed. SGLang pairs a frontend language (primitives for generation and parallelism control) with a runtime whose RadixAttention keeps an LRU cache of KV cache in a radix tree, reusing prefixes automatically across calls, and whose compressed finite state machines speed up constrained decoding for structured outputs. It reports up to 6.4 times higher throughput than state-of-the-art inference systems across agent control, logical reasoning, few-shot learning, JSON decoding, retrieval-augmented generation and multi-turn chat on large language and multi-modal models. The abstract is the record basis; the paper body was not read.

records.title: Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks
records.authors: Guangxuan Xiao, Yuandong Tian, Beidi Chen, Song Han, Mike Lewis
records.institution: MIT; Meta AI; Carnegie Mellon University
records.verification: abstract read 2026-11-03; paper body left unread.
records.relevance: The fix that lets a finite-context model stream indefinitely at inference time. Streaming deployment (multi-round dialogue, long interactions) hits two walls: KV cache memory during decoding, and models that cannot generalise beyond their training sequence length. Plain window attention, caching only the most recent tokens, collapses once text exceeds the cache size. The paper's observation is the attention sink: initial tokens attract strong attention scores even when semantically unimportant, so keeping just those initial tokens' KV (four suffice) alongside the sliding window largely restores window attention's performance. The resulting StreamingLLM framework lets Llama-2, MPT, Falcon and Pythia models do stable language modelling up to 4 million tokens and beyond with no fine-tuning, up to 22.2 times faster than the sliding-window recomputation baseline, and a dedicated sink token added during pre-training helps further. The abstract is the record basis; the paper body was not read.

records.title: DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning
records.verification: abstract read 2026-11-03; report body left unread.
records.relevance: The report that made inference-time reasoning the frontier: instead of scaling training, spend more compute at inference on longer chains of thought. DeepSeek-R1-Zero shows reasoning behaviour can be incentivised by large-scale reinforcement learning alone, with no supervised fine-tuning first: self-reflection, verification and dynamic strategy adaptation emerge from reward, and the model improves markedly on verifiable mathematics, coding competition and STEM tasks versus models trained on human demonstrations. DeepSeek-R1 adds multi-stage training and cold-start data to fix readability and language mixing, reaches performance comparable to OpenAI o1-1217 on reasoning tasks, and its reasoning is distilled into six open dense models from 1.5B to 70B parameters based on Qwen and Llama. The inference link is direct: capability here comes from generating far more tokens per answer at run time, which is why reasoning models changed the economics of serving. The abstract is the record basis; the report body was not read.

records.title: Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
records.authors: Charlie Snell, Jaehoon Lee, Kelvin Xu, Aviral Kumar
records.institution: University of California, Berkeley; Google DeepMind
records.verification: abstract read 2026-11-03; paper body left unread.
records.relevance: The scaling law for inference: for a fixed inference budget, how much can extra test-time compute improve a hard prompt, and when does it beat a bigger model? The paper studies two mechanisms, searching against dense process-based verifier reward models, and adaptively updating the model's response distribution at test time. In both cases the best approach depends critically on prompt difficulty, which motivates a compute-optimal strategy that allocates test-time compute adaptively per prompt. That strategy improves test-time compute efficiency by more than 4 times over a best-of-N baseline, and in a FLOPs-matched evaluation, test-time compute lets a smaller model outperform a 14 times larger model on problems where the smaller model already succeeds sometimes. The abstract is the record basis; the paper body was not read.

records.title: MLPerf Inference: Datacenter benchmark suite
records.verification: MLCommons benchmark page read 2026-11-03 (shown as V6.1); results tables left unread.
records.relevance: The industry-standard yardstick for inference speed, and the reason vendor latency and throughput claims can be compared at all. The MLPerf Inference: Datacenter suite measures how fast systems process inputs and produce results from a trained model, under scenarios defined by a standard load generator with latency constraints, throughput metrics and compliance rules. Each benchmark pairs a dataset with a quality target. Results are split into a Closed division (same reference model, apples-to-apples hardware and framework comparison) and an Open division (different model or retraining allowed), and into availability categories (Available, Preview, Research/Development/Internal). Power submissions measure full-system energy at the wall. The page read describes the suite's structure and rules; no individual system result is recorded because the results tables were left unread.

records.title: LLM inference prices have fallen rapidly but unequally across tasks
records.access: CC BY (per the page: free to use, distribute and reproduce with attribution)
records.verification: data insight page read 2026-11-03; chart values are SVG images that did not render as text, so no specific decline rate is recorded; underlying CSVs left unread.
records.relevance: The empirical price curve behind the claim that inference gets cheaper every year, with its method attached and its numbers deliberately withheld. Epoch combines LLM API prices and benchmark scores from Artificial Analysis and Epoch AI, identifies the lowest-priced models matching or exceeding a given benchmark score, and fits a log-linear regression of those prices over time, repeating the method across benchmarks (including MMLU and HumanEval) and performance thresholds (including GPT-3.5 and GPT-4o levels). The page's headline finding is that prices fell rapidly but unequally across tasks. No specific decline rate is recorded here because the chart values are SVG images that did not render as text; secondary summaries cite rates from 9 times to 900 times per year with a median near 50 times, but those figures were not read at origin and are not claimed. The page notes the analysis does not explicitly model what drives the drops, and that reduced profit margins may explain some of them without clear evidence. Underlying CSVs (updated 20 November 2025) were left unread.

records.title: MobileLLM: Optimizing Sub-billion Parameter Language Models for On-Device Use Cases
records.authors: Zechun Liu, Changsheng Zhao, Forrest Iandola, Chen Lai, Yuandong Tian, Igor Fedorov, Yunyang Xiong, Ernie Chang, Yangyang Shi, Raghuraman Krishnamoorthi, Liangzhen Lai, Vikas Chandra
records.verification: abstract read 2026-11-03; paper body left unread.
records.relevance: The architecture case for running capable models on a phone instead of in a data centre, driven by cloud costs and latency. For sub-billion-parameter models, architecture matters more than data or parameter count. MobileLLM uses deep and thin architectures with embedding sharing and grouped-query attention, beating preceding 125M and 350M state-of-the-art models by 2.7 and 4.3 percent accuracy. An immediate block-wise weight-sharing variant, MobileLLM-LS, adds a further 0.7 and 0.8 percent with no increase in model size and only marginal latency overhead. The family also improves markedly on chat benchmarks and comes close to Llama-2 7B on API calling tasks, showing small models can cover common on-device uses. The abstract is the record basis; the paper body was not read.

records.title: LLM.int8(): 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale
records.authors: Tim Dettmers, Mike Lewis, Younes Belkada, Luke Zettlemoyer
records.institution: University of Washington; Meta AI; Hugging Face
records.verification: abstract read 2026-11-03; paper body left unread.
records.relevance: The first method to run 175-billion-parameter models in 8-bit with no accuracy loss. Inference memory is the binding constraint for large transformers, and naive 8-bit quantisation breaks at scale because of emergent large-magnitude outlier features that dominate attention and predictions. LLM.int8() combines vector-wise quantisation, with separate normalisation constants per inner product, with a mixed-precision decomposition that isolates the outlier feature dimensions (about 0.1 percent of values) into a 16-bit multiplication while more than 99.9 percent of values multiply in 8-bit. The result halves inference memory while retaining full-precision performance, so a 175B checkpoint can be loaded, converted to Int8 and used immediately, putting OPT-175B and BLOOM on a single server with consumer GPUs. The abstract is the record basis; the paper body was not read.

records.relevance: The management-system standard for AI, which ISO calls the world's first AI management system standard. It specifies requirements and gives guidance for establishing, implementing, maintaining and continually improving an AI management system (AIMS) inside an organisation: the set of interrelated elements that establish policies, objectives and processes for the responsible development, provision or use of AI systems. It applies to organisations of any size that develop, provide or use AI-based products or services, across industries, including the public sector and non-profits. It follows Plan-Do-Check-Act and manages AI risks and opportunities organisation-wide rather than per application. ISO's listed benefits are a framework for managing risk and opportunities, demonstrating responsible use of AI, traceability, transparency and reliability, and cost savings and efficiency gains. records.relevance: The process standard for building ethics into system design instead of auditing it afterwards. It sets out processes by which organisations can include consideration of ethical values throughout concept exploration and development, supports management and engineering in transparent communication with selected stakeholders for ethical values elicitation and prioritisation, and requires traceability of ethical values through an operational concept, value propositions and value dispositions in the system design, with processes for traceability in the concept of operations, ethical requirements and ethical risk-based design. records.title: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) 1.0
records.authors: National Institute of Standards and Technology
records.institution: National Institute of Standards and Technology
records.verification: NIST overview page and AIRC executive summary read 2026-11-03; framework body left unread.
records.relevance: The voluntary US framework that most organisational AI governance now references, whether or not it is adopted wholesale. It is intended for voluntary use, to better manage risks to individuals, organisations and society associated with AI and to improve the ability to incorporate trustworthiness considerations into the design, development, use and evaluation of AI products, services and systems. Released 26 January 2023, it was developed through a consensus-driven, open, transparent and collaborative process including a Request for Information, several drafts for public comment and workshops, led by NIST's Information Technology Laboratory AI Program with the private and public sectors. Companions include the AI RMF Playbook, Roadmap, Crosswalk and Perspectives, and NIST launched the Trustworthy and Responsible AI Resource Center on 30 March 2023. The framework is intended to be voluntary, rights-preserving, non-sector-specific and use-case agnostic. Its Core has four functions, govern, map, measure and manage, with govern applying to all stages of an organisation's AI risk management and the other three applied in system-specific contexts and lifecycle stages; its trustworthiness characteristics are valid and reliable, safe, secure and resilient, accountable and transparent, explainable and interpretable, privacy enhanced, and fair with harmful biases managed. The NIST page also states AI RMF 1.0 is being revised as part of the White House AI Action Plan, with a concept note released 7 April 2026 for an AI RMF Profile on Trustworthy AI in Critical Infrastructure. Category and subcategory counts appearing in third-party summaries are not recorded here because only the overview and executive summary were read. The pages are the record basis; the framework body was not read.

records.title: Towards a Standard for Identifying and Managing Bias in Artificial Intelligence
records.authors: Reva Schwartz, Apostol Vassilev, Kristen Greene, Lori Perine, Andrew Burt, Patrick Hall
records.institution: National Institute of Standards and Technology
records.verification: executive summary read 2026-11-03; body left unread.
records.relevance: NIST's first step toward a bias standard, and the clearest statement in this batch that bias is a socio-technical problem, not a dataset bug. The publication takes a socio-technical perspective and surfaces the salient issues in AI bias as a first step toward detailed socio-technical guidance. It describes the stakes and challenge of bias in AI and how it chips away at public trust; identifies three categories of bias in AI, systemic, statistical and human, and how and where they contribute to harms; describes three broad challenges for mitigating bias, datasets, testing and evaluation, and human factors including test, evaluation, validation and verification (TEVV); and introduces preliminary guidance. Bias is neither new nor unique to AI, and zero risk of bias is not possible. NIST intends to develop methods for increasing assurance, governance and practice improvements for identifying, understanding, measuring, managing and reducing bias. NIST Special Publication 1270, 86 pages, March 2022. The executive summary is the record basis; the body was not read.

records.title: The next phase of the AI Standards Hub (AISH)
records.institution: National Physical Laboratory; British Standards Institution
records.verification: NPL news page read 2026-11-03.
records.relevance: The UK's standards-participation vehicle, at the moment its leadership changes hands. Going forward, the National Physical Laboratory (NPL) and the British Standards Institution (BSI) will lead the AI Standards Hub, while the Alan Turing Institute steps back from its leadership role as it transitions to a new mission focused on AI for national resilience. Background coverage places the Hub's founding in 2022 as part of the UK's National AI Strategy, as a partnership of the Alan Turing Institute, BSI and NPL supported by the UK Government through DSIT; that founding history is background, not the subject of the NPL page read. records.relevance: The impact-assessment companion to the management-system standard: 42001 tells an organisation to assess consequences, 42005 tells it how. It provides guidance for organisations conducting AI system impact assessments, focused on understanding how AI systems and their foreseeable applications may affect individuals, groups or society at large. It supports transparency, accountability and trust in AI by helping organisations identify, evaluate and document potential impacts throughout the AI system lifecycle. It is for any organisation developing, providing or using AI systems, regardless of sector or size, that wants to assess and manage the potential impacts of its AI systems on people and society. It complements ISO/IEC 42001 (AI management systems), ISO/IEC 38507 (AI governance) and ISO/IEC 23894 (AI risk management) by focusing specifically on the societal and human impacts of AI. It recommends performing assessments throughout the AI system lifecycle, from design and development to deployment and post-market monitoring, and updating them as needed. ISO's listed benefits are stronger stakeholder trust through transparent impact documentation, responsible innovation addressing social and ethical risks, alignment with governance, risk and compliance frameworks, better internal decision-making and accountability, and consistency and clarity in impact reporting.
